\chapter{Face Words}
\label{ch:ml-face-words}
\hlchaptermodality{37}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my eye, ear, nose and mouth in Malayalam, and say which of the four the family agrees on almost completely and which one Kannada alone breaks from.}

Name kannu, chevi, mookku and vaay, run the near-total four-way match on eye against chevi's three-against-one split on ear, and recall that Chapter 33 already named vaay once only to rule it out of vaayikkuka.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kaṇṇŭ]{\ml{കണ്ണ്} (kaṇṇŭ) — \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} the same word four times over}

\label{lesson:ML-C37-kannu}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{തല}}, \textbf{\ml{കൈ}} — head and hand, taught long ago, and nothing more of the body since, twenty-four chapters ago. This chapter adds four words to that short list, starting above the nose.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{കണ്ണ്}} — \emph{kaṇṇŭ} — \textbf{eye}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{കണ്ണ്}.} — \emph{ente kaṇṇŭ.} — \textquotedblleft{}My eye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{കണ്ണ്}} continues \textbf{Proto-Dravidian *kaṇ}, \textquotedblleft{}eye.\textquotedblright{} Tamil \textbf{\ta{கண்}} (\emph{kaṇ}) sits right beside it; Telugu \textbf{\te{కన్ను}} (\emph{kannu}) and Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಕಣ್ಣು}} (\emph{kaṇṇu}) sit closer still, both almost identical to Malayalam's own form. Four languages that otherwise pull apart on nearly everything — tense marking, half their everyday vocabulary, even the shape of their scripts — agree almost completely on this one word. It joins \textbf{\ml{തല}} and \textbf{\ml{കൈ}}, met earlier, as the third body word, and the first to show this exact, near-total four-way match.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ente kaṇṇŭ\textquotedblright{} — my eye
  \item the four sisters, nearly one word — \textquotedblleft{}kaṇṇŭ … kaṇ … kannu … kaṇṇu\textquotedblright{}
  \item three body words now — \textquotedblleft{}thala, kai, kaṇṇŭ\textquotedblright{}
  \item family, then body — \textquotedblleft{}makan, makaḷ … kaṇṇŭ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my eye.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ente kaṇṇŭ}.) Which three sisters come closest to matching Malayalam's word? (\textbf{All three} — Tamil \emph{kaṇ}, Telugu and Kannada both \emph{ka(ṇ)ṇu} — a near-total four-way match.) Name the body words you have now. (\emph{Thala}, head; \emph{kai}, hand; \emph{kaṇṇŭ}, eye.) Name the previous chapter's son and daughter words. (\emph{Makan}, \emph{makaḷ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cevi]{\ml{ചെവി} (cevi) — \textquotedblleft{}ear,\textquotedblright{} where Kannada is the odd one out}

\label{lesson:ML-C37-chevi}



\begin{quote}
The four-way match on \emph{kaṇṇŭ} was close to perfect. This word breaks the pattern — but not the way you'd expect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ചെവി}} — \emph{cevi} — \textbf{ear}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{ചെവി}.} — \emph{ente cevi.} — \textquotedblleft{}My ear.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ചെവി}} continues \textbf{Proto-Dravidian *kewi}, \textquotedblleft{}ear.\textquotedblright{} Tamil \textbf{\ta{செவி}} (\emph{cevi}) and Telugu \textbf{\te{చెవి}} (\emph{cevi}) match Malayalam almost exactly — all three softened the old initial \emph{\textbf{k-}} into a \emph{\textbf{c-/ch-}} sound before this particular front vowel. \textbf{Kannada alone kept the older sound}: \textbf{\ka{ಕಿವಿ}} (\emph{kivi}), \emph{k-} untouched. So this time it is not Malayalam standing apart from three sisters, the way \emph{kuṭumbaṁ}'s dressed \emph{-aṁ} did — it is Kannada, holding onto the sound the other three let go of.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ente cevi\textquotedblright{} — my ear
  \item three softened, one not — \textquotedblleft{}cevi, cevi, cevi … kivi\textquotedblright{}
  \item two face words now — \textquotedblleft{}kaṇṇŭ, cevi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the closest family match — \textquotedblleft{}makaḷ, makaḷ\textquotedblright{} — Malayalam, Tamil
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my ear.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ente cevi}.) Which three sisters agree on this word, and which one differs? (\textbf{Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu} agree — \textbf{Kannada} alone keeps the older \emph{k-} sound, \emph{kivi}.) Why is that the reverse of what you might expect? (Usually Malayalam is the one that goes its own way; here Malayalam sides with the majority and \textbf{Kannada} is the outlier.) Which earlier word was identical between Malayalam and Tamil, sound for sound? (\emph{\textbf{\ml{മകൾ}}}, \emph{makaḷ}, daughter.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūkkŭ]{\ml{മൂക്ക്} (mūkkŭ) — \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} and the same softening you met on \textquotedblleft{}son\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C37-mookku}



\begin{quote}
Two face words down. This one brings back a sound-change from the last chapter, in a new place.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{മൂക്ക്}} — \emph{mūkkŭ} — \textbf{nose}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{മൂക്ക്}.} — \emph{ente mūkkŭ.} — \textquotedblleft{}My nose.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{മൂക്ക്}} is native Dravidian, close to Tamil \textbf{\ta{மூக்கு}} (\emph{mūkku}) and Telugu \textbf{\te{ముక్కు}} (\emph{mukku}). Kannada shows \textbf{\ka{ಮೂಗು}} (\emph{mūgu}) — the very same \emph{-k-} to \emph{-g-} softening you already met between Malayalam's \textbf{\ml{മകൻ}} and Kannada's \textbf{\ka{ಮಗ}}. It is a small, recurring signature: wherever Malayalam and Tamil hold a \emph{-k-} between vowels, Kannada is likely to have worn it down to a \emph{-g-}, whether the word is a family word or a body word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ente mūkkŭ\textquotedblright{} — my nose
  \item the recurring softening — \textquotedblleft{}makan, maga … mūkkŭ, mūgu\textquotedblright{}
  \item three face words — \textquotedblleft{}kaṇṇŭ, cevi, mūkkŭ\textquotedblright{}
  \item three against one, once more — \textquotedblleft{}cevi, cevi, cevi … kivi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my nose.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ente mūkkŭ}.) What does Kannada's \textbf{\ka{ಮೂಗು}} (\emph{mūgu}) show, that you already saw once before? (\textbf{The same \emph{-k-} to \emph{-g-} softening} as \emph{makan} $\to$ \emph{maga}.) Name the three face words so far. (\emph{Kaṇṇŭ}, eye; \emph{cevi}, ear; \emph{mūkkŭ}, nose.) Which sister alone breaks the family's agreement on \emph{cevi}? (\textbf{Kannada}, \emph{kivi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vāy]{\ml{വായ്} (vāy) — \textquotedblleft{}mouth,\textquotedblright{} the word an earlier lesson named only to rule out}

\label{lesson:ML-C37-vaay}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Ñān malayāḷaṁ vāyikkunnu}, \textquotedblleft{}I read Malayalam\textquotedblright{} — and an earlier lesson told you the obvious-looking mouth-word inside it wasn't really there. Here, at last, is the real one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{വായ്}} — \emph{vāy} — \textbf{mouth}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{വായ്}.} — \emph{ente vāy.} — \textquotedblleft{}My mouth.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{വായ്}} is native Dravidian, matching Tamil \textbf{\ta{வாய்}} (\emph{vāy}) almost exactly. Kannada shows the family's own \textbf{v‑to‑b} shift here, \textbf{\ka{ಬಾಯಿ}} (\emph{bāyi}) — the same shift, in reverse direction from the \emph{k}‑to‑\emph{c} softening \emph{chevi} showed you, that turns up across the family's native vocabulary. Telugu's everyday word, \textbf{\te{నోరు}} (\emph{nōru}), is a different root altogether.

An earlier lesson already put \textbf{\ml{വായ്}} on the table once — as the wrong answer. \textbf{\ml{വായിക്കുക}} (\emph{vāyikkuka}, \textquotedblleft{}to read\textquotedblright{}) looks built on this very word, and Gundert's dictionary says it isn't: the trail runs instead to Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{वच्}} (\emph{vac}), \textquotedblleft{}to speak.\textquotedblright{} That lesson named \emph{vāy} only to set it aside. This is the word itself, finally taught for what it actually means.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ente vāy\textquotedblright{} — my mouth
  \item the cousins — \textquotedblleft{}vāy … bāyi … nōru\textquotedblright{} — Malayalam/Tamil, Kannada, Telugu
  \item the false trail, named again — \textquotedblleft{}vāyikkuka\textquotedblright{} is NOT built on \textquotedblleft{}vāy\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four face words — \textquotedblleft{}kaṇṇŭ, cevi, mūkkŭ, vāy\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my mouth.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ente vāy}.) Which earlier lesson already mentioned \emph{vāy}, and why? (\textbf{The \emph{vāyikkuka} lesson}, to rule out that \emph{vāyikkuka}, \textquotedblleft{}to read,\textquotedblright{} is built on it.) What does Kannada's \emph{bāyi} show? (\textbf{The family's \emph{v}-to-\emph{b} shift.}) Name all four face words. (\emph{Kaṇṇŭ}, eye; \emph{cevi}, ear; \emph{mūkkŭ}, nose; \emph{vāy}, mouth.)
\end{tcolorbox}
